subtype: Approach: ration supplies and check on stranded relatives [Revision]
passage: By the second morning the corridor floor of the hostel was under an inch of water and the mess had shut. Hrithik went from room to room on the third floor and counted: nine packets of biscuits, two bags of puffed rice, a tin of tea leaves and twenty-two bottles of water among fourteen students. He had eaten a big breakfast as usual, and now the numbers made his stomach tighten. "We planned as if it was one day," he told Avni from the next room. Together they rewrote it: three small meals, water in cups, and a chart taped to the door. Then they tried every way of reaching home. The hostel landline crackled, texts kept failing, and near midnight one finally went through to Hrithik's cousin in the next district.

qa.q: How many bottles of water did Hrithik count?
qa.a: Hrithik counted twenty-two bottles of water among fourteen students.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling as he counted the supplies?
qa.a: Hrithik felt anxious, his stomach tightening as he realised the plan had been for one day.

qa.q: What else could the group do to stretch supplies, and why?
qa.a: They could ask the other floors and the warden about their stock and plan together, because a shared count shows how long everything must last.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt as the plan came together?
qa.a: Avni probably felt relieved to have a clear plan and stayed worried until a message finally got through.

grounding: Illustrates a person trapped by floods counting food and water, replanning consumption around the limit, and trying every channel to reach relatives.

passage:
Dear Samir,
Thank you for all your calls last week. I can finally write properly.
When the water trapped us on the first floor, I panicked the first night. We ate dinner as usual, drank as much as we liked, and kept the lights on until the inverter died.
The next morning I realised we didn't know how long this would last. So I counted everything: nine litres of drinking water, a kilo of rice, bread, two packets of biscuits, some fruit. I divided it for two more days for four of us, with water first for Nani. No more cooking rice that wasted water.
Then relatives. Phones barely worked, so I sent short texts instead of calls, since those got through. I reached Mama in Silchar and asked him to check on Mami's family downstream. He did; they were safe.
The boat came on day three. We still had a litre left.
Bhavna

qa.q: How much drinking water did Bhavna count?
qa.a: Bhavna counted nine litres of drinking water.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel on the first night, and what changed the next morning?
qa.a: Bhavna panicked on the first night, then felt more in control after counting everything and planning for two days.

qa.q: What else could Bhavna's family keep ready for next time?
qa.a: They could keep a stock of water and dry food on the upper floor before the monsoon, so rationing starts with more.

qa.q: How might Mama in Silchar have felt getting Bhavna's text?
qa.a: Mama likely felt relieved to hear from Bhavna and useful when asked to check on Mami's family.

grounding: Shows the person, trapped by floods for two days, counting food and water, planning consumption and reaching relatives through whatever channel worked.

passage:
"Baljeet, you asked what I learned in the flood. So here it is, from me, Kavitha, stuck on a roof for two days with my parents and a goat.
The first evening, we ate like it was normal. Then I looked at what we'd carried up: six bottles of water, a bag of flattened rice, some jaggery, a few bananas. And I thought, what if it's three days? Nobody knows.
So I changed everything. I lined up the bottles and made a rule: small sips, Amma's medicine water first. The rice and jaggery split into six small meals. I tied the bag to the water tank so it wouldn't slide.
Our phones were almost dead. Calls wouldn't go through, but texts sometimes did. So I switched off both phones and turned one on every three hours to send one message to my uncle and check for replies.
On day two the reply came: the rescue boat was coming."

qa.q: What did Kavitha tie to the water tank?
qa.a: Kavitha tied the food bag to the water tank so it wouldn't slide.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel after the first evening?
qa.a: Kavitha felt worried and uncertain, thinking it might last three days with nobody knowing.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha do next time before the water rises?
qa.a: Kavitha could move more water and food up to the roof early and charge phones fully, so rationing starts with more.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's uncle have felt receiving the messages?
qa.a: The uncle likely felt anxious but relieved each time a message came through, and able to pass on news of the rescue boat.

grounding: Shows the person trapped by floods rationing food and water for an unknown stretch and reaching relatives through texts when calls failed.
